turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, grab a seat. Sorry about the wait — we've been flat out this arvo.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): That's alright. Um, I don't know, doctor, I feel a bit silly coming in. I've just been so tired.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. How long's it been?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. Six months? Maybe longer, I can't pin the start. I figured it was work — I'm a project manager, desk all day, deadlines are brutal. And I'm fifty-two, so maybe it's just age.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Could be either. Is it that you can't get going, or you're wrecked after the day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, sort of. I sleep heaps, nine hours easy, and I still wake up tired. It's not that I can't get to sleep.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feeling cold as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I blamed the office aircon. Well, actually it's at home too, even with the doona on. A few months.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your weight?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I've put on that much.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes fitting the same?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. Jeans are two sizes up, so yes I have. Five or six kilos. I don't know exactly — I gave up on the scales.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the bowels?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Constipated, honestly. Maybe three times a week, and it used to be every morning. No blood in the stool.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain with that?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain really. Just slow, hard to get going. Sorry, that's grim.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your mood sitting in all this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. I don't enjoy the footy or dinner with my sister like I did. I pinned it on work being hectic. I don't know if I'm depressed, doctor.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you taken anything for the bowels, or for your mood?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Coloxyl, from the chemist. One tablet a day for about a week, then I stopped because it didn't do much. Nothing for mood. I never have.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Tired, cold, weight up, sluggish bowels, low mood — that pattern can be an underactive thyroid. Any thyroid disease in the family?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum had it. Underactive, I think. She was on tablets for years. She died a few years back, so I don't know the fine detail.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And has your own thyroid been checked?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Years ago, yeah. The old GP did a blood test and they said it was borderline. I never followed it up. I don't know the number, and I couldn't say when it was.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so we've got 'borderline' as you remember it, not a number I can rely on. Has anyone ever actually diagnosed you with a thyroid condition?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I'm pretty well apart from this. Oh, random one — I reckon the parking meter's about to run out.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your skin and hair?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Skin's a bit dry. Hair, I don't know, doctor. Maybe there's more in the brush. I'm not sure, so I wouldn't trust that.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put down the dry skin and leave the hair. On examination the thyroid isn't enlarged, there's no lump, the heart sounds are fine, and your ankles aren't swollen.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So is this just age? I don't know, doctor. I had a coffee on the way, if you're doing bloods — do I need to fast?

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to fast, the coffee's fine. I'm not calling it hypothyroidism today. The working idea is an underactive thyroid, given the symptoms and your mum, but burning out at work stays on the list. I won't start thyroxine on a guess.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I just want to feel like myself again.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll order a thyroid function test and a full blood count today. If those thyroid numbers are out of whack and this hasn't settled, we might do an ultrasound of the thyroid — I am not booking that now.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And the, um, not going to the toilet. Anything I should do meanwhile?

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep your fluids up and add some fibre, pears or oats. If your mood drops hard, or you can't get out of bed, come back sooner or ring the clinic, don't sit on it. Otherwise let's see you in a couple of weeks once the results are in — reception can book that as you leave.

spec.situation: Middle-aged person tired and cold for months, weight up, constipated, low mood; pins it on work and age; mother had thyroid disease; one old thyroid test result recalled wrongly ('borderline, they said'). Blood test planned.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Constipation supported, but '3 times a week' describes bowel motions frequency, not constipation frequency.
bad.text: constipation (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, frequency=about 3 times a week, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Weight gain quantified as about 5 to 6 kg, with jeans now two sizes bigger.
Constipation detail is recorded wrongly: patient said bowels are now about three times a week, whereas previously they were every morning.
Previous thyroid blood test was done years ago by the old GP and was recalled by the patient as 'borderline'; patient did not know the value or when it was done and never followed it up.
Doctor specifically said they were not diagnosing hypothyroidism today and would not start thyroxine on a guess.
Safety-net advice included to come back sooner or ring the clinic if mood drops hard, and specifically 'don't sit on it'.
